label: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
statement: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.
quote: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.
scope: number-based systems treated in traditional science and mathematics

label: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
statement: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.
quote: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.
scope: base-2 digit sequences of powers of 3

label: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
statement: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.
quote: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.
scope: fractional parts of (3/2)^n

label: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
statement: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.
quote: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.
scope: simple piecewise arithmetic maps on whole numbers

label: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
statement: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.
quote: But despite fundamental differences like this in underlying rules, the overall behavior produced by systems based on numbers is still very similar to what one sees for example in cellular automata.
scope: number-based systems compared with cellular automata and other simple programs

label: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
statement: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.
quote: Localized structures are visible, but the overall pattern never seems to take on any kind of simple repetitive form.
scope: base-2 reverse-and-add iteration from particular starting numbers

label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
statement: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.
quote: even though the rules ultimately involve only addition and subtraction, they nevertheless correspond to programs that are capable of producing behavior of great complexity.
scope: nested recursive integer sequences (Hofstadter-like sequences)

label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
statement: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
quote: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.
scope: the sequence of prime numbers

label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
statement: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
quote: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.
scope: integer sequences defined by simple number-theoretic properties

label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
statement: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
quote: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.
scope: digit sequence of pi in any base

label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
statement: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
quote: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.
scope: digit expansions of real numbers

label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
statement: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
quote: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.
scope: digit sequences of square roots of non-square integers

label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
statement: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
quote: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
scope: digit sequences of higher roots, logarithms and exponentials of small integers

label: Roots never have nested digit sequences
statement: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
quote: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.
scope: digit expansions of algebraic numbers obtained as roots

label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
statement: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
quote: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.
scope: continued fraction expansions of common irrational numbers

label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
statement: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
quote: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations are often in some intrinsic sense complex, independent of the particular representation that one uses to look at them.
scope: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations, across number representations

label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
statement: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
quote: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
scope: zero sets of sums of two sinusoids

label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
statement: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
quote: in no real sense is any randomness actually being generated by the evolution of this system. Instead, it is just that randomness that was inserted in the digit sequence of the original number shows up in the results one gets.
scope: the shift map and similar chaotic maps that act as digit shifts

label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
statement: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
quote: a crucial discovery in this book is that systems like (a) and (b) on pages 150 and 151 can show behavior that seems in many respects random even when their initial conditions show no sign of randomness and are in fact extremely simple.
scope: simple one-dimensional iterated maps on [0, 1]

label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
statement: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
quote: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems and iterated maps

label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
statement: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
quote: despite the presence of continuous gray levels, the behavior that is produced exhibits the same kind of complexity that we have seen in many ordinary cellular automata and other systems with discrete underlying elements.
scope: one-dimensional continuous-valued cellular automata

label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
statement: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
quote: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.
scope: history of mathematical modeling in physics and other sciences

label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
statement: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
quote: it is certainly not that nature fundamentally follows these abstractions.
scope: fundamental laws of physics

label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
statement: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
quote: we now know that the same kind of behavior can also occur in completely continuous systems such as partial differential equations.
scope: one-dimensional nonlinear partial differential equations

label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
statement: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.
quote: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.
scope: continuous versus discrete dynamical systems

label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
statement: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
quote: I suspect that essentially all of the various phenomena that we have observed in discrete systems in the past several chapters can in fact also be found even in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
scope: continuous systems such as continuous cellular automata, iterated maps and partial differential equations

label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
statement: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
quote: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.
scope: simple programs (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems) in one, two and three dimensions

label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
statement: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
quote: if one looks at the evolution of a one-dimensional slice through each two-dimensional pattern the results one gets are strikingly similar to what we have seen in ordinary one-dimensional cellular automata.
scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata from a single seed

label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
statement: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
quote: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.
scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata with 8 neighbors

label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
statement: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
quote: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.
scope: two-dimensional growth-type cellular automata

label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
statement: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
quote: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.
scope: three-dimensional cellular automata

label: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
statement: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).
quote: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.
scope: two-dimensional Turing machines with two to four head states and two colors

label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
statement: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.
quote: with this kind of setup, it is ultimately inevitable that all the patterns produced must have a completely regular nested structure.
scope: neighbor-independent two-dimensional substitution systems and iterated geometric replacement rules

label: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
statement: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.
quote: in traditional fractal geometry the idea of interaction between elements is not considered—so that all patterns that are produced have a purely nested form.
scope: fractal geometry and two-dimensional neighbor-dependent substitution systems

label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
statement: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.
quote: using the same principles an array with any number of dimensions can easily be obtained.
scope: directed networks with out-degree two

label: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth
statement: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).
quote: even the total number of nodes at each step can vary in a way that seems in many respects completely random.
scope: network systems with local rewiring and node-insertion rules

label: Network systems may underlie the structure of space and spacetime
statement: Some network systems will likely turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
quote: I suspect that some of these systems will in the end turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
scope: fundamental structure of physical space and spacetime

label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
statement: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.
quote: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.
scope: multiway (non-deterministic string rewriting) systems with simple rules

label: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
statement: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).
quote: even when such growth leads to a certain amount of apparent randomness it typically in the end seems to exhibit some form of repetition.
scope: slowly growing multiway systems

label: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
statement: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.
quote: multiway systems can in effect build up their own pattern of connections in time—and this pattern can often be quite complicated.
scope: multiway systems

label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
statement: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
quote: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.
scope: one-dimensional local constraint systems (one-dimensional subshifts of finite type)

label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
statement: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
quote: among the 3,527,988,252 that remain, it turns out that every single one can be satisfied by a simple repetitive pattern.
scope: two-dimensional two-color constraints on five-cell (von Neumann) neighborhood templates

label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
statement: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
quote: But in a system that is based on constraints, there is no such direct procedure, and instead one must in effect always go outside of the system to work out what patterns can occur.
scope: systems defined by constraints versus explicit evolution rules

label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
statement: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
quote: after examining more than 18 million of them, one finally discovers the system shown on the facing page. And in this system, unlike all others before it, no repetitive pattern is possible; the only pattern that satisfies the constraint is the non-repetitive nested pattern shown in the picture.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition

label: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
statement: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.
quote: of the millions of these that I have tested, none have forced anything more complicated than the kind of nested behavior seen on the previous page.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition

label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
statement: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.
quote: a system with 56 allowed templates in which the only pattern satisfying the constraint is a complex and largely random one, derived from the rule 30 cellular automaton.
scope: two-dimensional constraints on 3×3 neighborhoods

label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
statement: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
quote: it seems that almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns.
scope: constraint-based systems compared with rule-based simple programs

label: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
statement: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.
quote: the fact that traditional science and mathematics tends to concentrate on equations that operate like constraints provides yet another reason for their failure to identify the fundamental phenomenon of complexity that I discuss in this book.
scope: methods of traditional science and mathematics

label: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
statement: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.
quote: many systems spontaneously tend to organize themselves, so that even with completely random initial conditions they end up producing behavior that has many features that are not at all random.
scope: cellular automata and similar simple programs started from random initial conditions

label: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes
statement: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3), and interacting localized structures (class 4).
quote: among all kinds of cellular automata, it seems that the patterns which arise can almost always be assigned quite easily to one of just four basic classes illustrated below.
scope: all kinds of cellular automata evolved from random initial conditions

label: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways
statement: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
quote: class 4 involves a mixture of order and randomness: localized structures are produced which on their own are fairly simple, but these structures move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes
statement: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.
quote: most of these properties were closely correlated with the classes that I had already identified. Indeed, in trying to predict detailed properties of a particular cellular automaton, it was often enough just to know what class the cellular automaton was in.
scope: cellular automata in general

label: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule
statement: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.
quote: In most cases there is no easy way to do this, and in fact there is little choice but just to run the cellular automaton and see what it does.
scope: predicting cellular automaton behavior class from rule specification

label: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity
statement: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.
quote: Class 4 systems are then in the middle: for the activity that they show neither dies out completely, as in class 2, nor remains at the high level seen in class 3.
scope: sequences of cellular automaton rules, both discrete and continuous

label: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes
statement: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.
quote: But it seems that this behavior falls into essentially the same four classes that we have already seen in ordinary cellular automata.
scope: continuous cellular automata with a smoothly varying rule parameter

label: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes
statement: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.
quote: Indeed, by looking at such slices one can readily identify the very same four classes of behavior as in one-dimensional cellular automata.
scope: two-dimensional cellular automata

label: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
statement: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.
quote: In class 1, changes always die out, and in fact exactly the same final state is reached regardless of what initial conditions were used. In class 2, changes may persist, but they always remain localized in a small region of the system.
scope: cellular automata of all four classes

label: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information
statement: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.
quote: it is often possible to understand some of the most important features of systems that occur in nature just by looking at how their handling of information corresponds to what we have seen in the basic classes of systems that we have identified here.
scope: natural systems in general

label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
statement: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.
quote: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.
scope: finite-state deterministic discrete systems

label: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication
statement: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.
quote: the absence of long-range communication effectively forces each part of a class 2 system to behave as if it were a system of limited size.
scope: class 2 cellular automata

label: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
statement: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.
quote: In general, a rapid increase with size is characteristic of class 3 behavior. Of the elementary rules, however, only rule 45 seems to yield periods that always stay close to the maximum of 2n.
scope: elementary cellular automata on cyclic lattices of size n

label: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
statement: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.
quote: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.
scope: class 3 cellular automata such as rule 30 and rule 22

label: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
statement: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.
quote: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.
scope: additive cellular automata (rule 90) versus non-additive class 3 rules (rule 22)

label: Intrinsic randomness generation makes large-scale behavior stable
statement: Systems that intrinsically generate randomness, like rule 22 or rule 30, produce the same overall random behavior with the same large-scale properties whatever their initial conditions, giving them a fundamental stability that he says underlies the apparent stability of many systems in nature.
quote: By intrinsically generating randomness such systems in a sense have a certain fundamental stability: for whatever is done to their initial conditions, they still give the same overall random behavior, with the same large-scale properties.
scope: intrinsically random cellular automata and natural systems with apparent stability

label: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
statement: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.
quote: in any cellular automaton it is inevitable that initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever will lead to simple repetitive behavior.
scope: all cellular automata with spatially periodic initial conditions

label: Special initial conditions often make one cellular automaton emulate another
statement: It is common for a cellular automaton to have special initial conditions under which it behaves exactly like some other cellular automaton; for example rule 126 behaves like rule 90 when started from paired-cell blocks, and class 3 rules can thereby act like class 2 rules.
quote: it turns out to be quite common for there to exist special initial conditions for one cellular automaton that make it behave just like some other cellular automaton.
scope: cellular automata and their block emulations

label: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
statement: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.
quote: And this can be achieved in only two ways: either the pattern must be essentially uniform, or it must have a nested structure—just like we see in rule 90.
scope: self-emulating cellular automata

label: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
statement: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.
quote: one can show that any rule that is additive will be able to emulate itself and will thus yield nested patterns. But there are rather few additive rules, and indeed with two colors and nearest neighbors the only fundamentally different ones are precisely rules 90 and 150.
scope: additive cellular automata, especially elementary rules

label: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
statement: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules started from all possible sequences.
quote: Indeed, this kind of rapid increase in network complexity is a general characteristic of most class 3 and 4 rules.
scope: one-dimensional cellular automata and the regular languages of their configurations

label: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever
statement: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
quote: Most of these structures eventually die out, sometimes in rather complicated ways. But a crucial feature of any class 4 systems is that there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist
statement: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.
quote: My experience with many different rules is that whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems
statement: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.
quote: it is a general feature of class 4 cellular automata that with appropriate initial conditions they can mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity
statement: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.
quote: So even though the individual structures in class 4 systems like rule 110 may behave in fairly repetitive ways, interactions between these structures can lead to behavior of immense complexity.
scope: rule 110 and other class 4 cellular automata

label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
statement: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
quote: And the crucial point is that I believe that this universality extends not only across simple programs, but also to systems in nature.
scope: simple programs and natural systems with different underlying components

label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
statement: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
quote: But from my investigations of simple programs I have come to the conclusion that one can in fact identify just three basic mechanisms for randomness, as illustrated in the pictures below.
scope: all systems, natural or computational, that show apparent randomness
